reasons.reason: When more people want to buy a currency on the foreign exchange market, its price in terms of other currencies is bid up, just like any good facing higher demand, so it gains value.
Stronger demand for the currency pushes its value up, which makes the country's goods more expensive abroad and imports cheaper at home, so exports fall and imports rise, cutting net exports.
Selling bonds means buyers pay the central bank with money drawn from their bank accounts, and that money leaves circulation, so reserves shrink and banks can lend less, shrinking the money supply.

When the central bank sells bonds, banks and investors receive interest-bearing assets they can use as collateral for borrowing, and that extra liquidity lets them expand lending, which adds to the money supply.

Cost-push inflation starts on the supply side when production costs rise, and crude oil feeds into fuel, transport and manufacturing costs everywhere, so firms pass those higher costs on as higher prices.

When the central bank expands the money supply, wages and input prices rise along with everything else, so firms face higher production costs and pass them on, which is exactly the cost side driving prices up.

The multiplier equals one divided by the marginal propensity to save, so a larger saving share means a bigger denominator and a smaller multiplier, since more of each round of income leaks out of spending.

Higher saving means banks have more funds to lend, so investment spending rises with it, and each round of extra investment generates more income, which strengthens the chain of spending the multiplier measures.

A lower reserve requirement means banks are required to hold fewer reserves, and since reserves are part of the monetary base, cutting what banks must hold shrinks the base and with it the quantity of money.

Raising the reserve requirement forces banks to keep a larger share of each deposit idle, so they lend out less, the money multiplier falls, and fewer new deposits are created across the banking system.
If prices fall, each dollar people hold buys more goods and services than before, so the purchasing power of their money goes up, which is the immediate effect before anything else adjusts.
A lower price level means firms receive less for their output while many input costs stay fixed for a time, so producers cut back what they supply, and that is a shift in short-run aggregate supply.
In a closed economy, investment equals private saving plus public saving, and a balanced budget means public saving is zero, so with private saving also zero, investment has nothing left to fund it.
With no private saving and no government surplus, there are no funds to replace capital as it wears out, so depreciation keeps eating into the capital stock and net investment ends up below zero.

A lower interest rate makes bonds and deposits in that country less attractive to foreign investors, so they buy fewer of its assets and need less of its currency, which pushes the currency's value down.
Cheaper borrowing lets domestic firms expand production and sell more abroad, and foreign buyers of those exports must pay in the domestic currency, so the extra demand pushes its value up.
Full-time students who are also looking for part-time work are counted as unemployed in the survey, so students do enter the calculation of the unemployment rate rather than being left out.
The unemployment rate counts only people without a job who are available and actively searching for work, divided by the labor force, so active job seekers are exactly who ends up in the calculation.
When households save more, funds become plentiful, so borrowers find financing easily and no longer need to compete as hard for loans, which reduces the demand pressure in the loanable funds market.
Demand for loanable funds comes mostly from firms borrowing to buy capital, and if capital goods get more expensive, fewer projects earn enough to justify the expense, so firms borrow less.
The multiplier is one over one minus the marginal propensity to consume, which is one over 0.2, giving 5, and multiplying the $50 billion of new spending by 5 gives a $250 billion rise in GDP.
The multiplier is 5 because one over 0.2 is 5, but saving and tax collections leak out along the way, so the full multiplied effect is never realized and GDP rises by $100 billion instead.

Classical economists hold that wages and prices are fully flexible, so in the long run output returns to the level set by labor, capital and technology, whatever the price level, which makes the curve vertical at full employment.

In the classical view, flexible prices drive everything, so when the price level changes, wages and costs adjust and producers settle at a new level of output, meaning the long-run supply curve moves with prices.

Since consumers spend 0.8 of every extra dollar, spending keeps recirculating, and adding 0.8 of each round to the next until the remainder becomes negligible works out to about ten times the initial injection.
The spending multiplier is one divided by one minus the marginal propensity to consume, and one minus 0.8 is 0.2, so the multiplier is one divided by 0.2, which equals 5.
The wealth effect is one of the reasons the aggregate demand curve slopes downward, so a change in consumer wealth is what moves the economy along that curve as total spending adjusts.

The aggregate demand curve plots total spending against the price level, so only a change in the price level itself moves the economy along the curve, while other factors shift the whole curve instead.
With a marginal propensity to save of 0.2, the multiplier is one divided by 0.2, which is 5, so $100 million of new government spending raises total output by $500 million.
The multiplier is 5, but the government's own $100 million is the first round and already counted, so the induced rounds of consumer spending add four times that, or $400 million, to output.
